workstream.title: Frontend and Accessibility: sandwich dpwnload manager

request.title: sandwich dpwnload manager
request.problem: Internet Download Manager is one of the most widely installed download software programs in the world.We’ve decided to build a new product that will be free, so no one will need to buy a subscription. It’s called “Sandwich Download Manager.”Offering the best internet download software on all devices and across all operating systems.I need to have a native version for Windows, a native version for Mac, and a native version for Linux.IDM is one of the most well-known download managers in the world. Most Windows users use IDM, but it’s paid software—if I’m not mistaken, it becomes paid after one month or three months. Given how widely people need this kind of download software, we want to build an open-source version of a similar product.And the plan is to release this product as open-source and free everywhere—put it on GitHub. The key point is that I want it to have a very easy UX and be very minimal, modern, and clean.
request.desiredOutcome: Ask the human product owner to choose an initial platform and bounded MVP before committing to three native applications; Windows-first is a hypothesis requiring approval, not a decided direction.

acceptanceCriteria.verification: Review a dated decision record attributed to the human product owner, with unresolved assumptions listed separately.

acceptanceCriteria.statement: The MVP specifies observable behavior for adding, pausing, resuming, cancelling, retrying, and completing downloads, including restart recovery and destination handling.
acceptanceCriteria.verification: Trace each behavior to an approved requirement and an independently verifiable acceptance scenario.

acceptanceCriteria.statement: The platform strategy states whether Windows, macOS, and Linux use shared or separate foundations and documents packaging, updating, browser integration, and maintenance implications.

acceptanceCriteria.statement: The open-source release model defines license, third-party dependency rules, contribution governance, security reporting, and binary release ownership.

acceptanceCriteria.statement: Usability and accessibility expectations are testable for the core download flow.

nonFunctionalRequirements.requirement: Core UI interactions remain responsive while multiple downloads are active, and download concurrency does not exhaust system resources.
nonFunctionalRequirements.verification: Define platform-specific budgets for UI responsiveness, CPU, memory, disk, and network use, then measure them under representative concurrent workloads.

nonFunctionalRequirements.requirement: Interrupted downloads and application restarts do not silently corrupt completed or partial files.
nonFunctionalRequirements.verification: Test network loss, process termination, restart, insufficient disk space, and server range-support variations with integrity checks.

nonFunctionalRequirements.requirement: Downloaded content, URLs, credentials, browser integration, updates, and release artifacts are handled using secure defaults.
nonFunctionalRequirements.verification: Perform threat modeling, dependency scanning, signed-release verification, secret-handling tests, and an independent security review before public distribution.

nonFunctionalRequirements.requirement: Telemetry is absent by default or transparent, minimized, and consent-based; sensitive URLs and credentials are not exposed in logs.
nonFunctionalRequirements.verification: Inspect defaults, data flows, retention behavior, logs, and user controls against an approved privacy specification.

nonFunctionalRequirements.requirement: Core workflows are operable without a pointer and expose meaningful status and controls to assistive technologies.
nonFunctionalRequirements.verification: Run automated checks plus manual keyboard and screen-reader scenarios on every supported platform.
